title: RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1999 FCA) SR&ED Case
subject: FCA review of SR&ED eligibility for spatial membrane panel research and evidentiary proof of systematic testing.
summary: RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (FCA, 1998) is a Federal Court of Appeal decision holding that, for Canadian taxpayers claiming SR&ED incentives under the Income Tax Act, documentary proof of repeatability is not an absolute legal prerequisite. Once testing, a new product and a technological advancement are proven, a rebuttable inference arises that the research was systematic.
metaDescription: Review the 1999 FCA SR&ED decision for RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen ([1999] 1 C.T.C. 132) and its impact on Canadian R&D tax credits.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in R I S - Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 DTC 5087 (Docket A-710-96, decided December 21, 1998) stands as a foundational appellate authority in Canada governing the evidentiary standard of proof for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives. Heard in Toronto on December 3, 1998, before Justices Strayer, Robertson, and Sexton, with unanimous Reasons for Judgment delivered by Justice Robertson, the ruling directly demarcates the legal boundary between statutory eligibility requirements and administrative documentation demands. Specifically, the appeal resolved whether a Canadian taxpayer is strictly obligated as a matter of law to adduce contemporaneous documentary evidence of "repeatable" experimental parameters to qualify for tax incentives under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act") and the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations"), even where independent evidence establishes that experimentation occurred and a genuine technological advancement was achieved.
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

The dispute originated in 1982 when Leonid Slonimsky (identified in the Tax Court of Canada decision as Leon Slonimsky, who died before trial), a professional engineer, and Daniel Dorcich, a businessman, conceived an engineering concept to develop an innovative concrete forming medium for cast-in-situ concrete construction, designated as a "spatial membrane panel". The technical objective of the spatial membrane panel was to overcome structural and material limitations in conventional poured-in-place concrete forming by simultaneously reducing construction fabrication costs and substantially increasing the thermal insulation quality of the cured concrete structure.

To finance and execute the development, an agreement was executed as of December 1, 1982, between Williams & Turner Consultants Inc. ("Consultants"), a manager of scientific research and development projects, and a newly incorporated Ontario numbered corporation, 541185 Ontario Inc. ("O Inc."), under which O Inc. undertook to perform the requisite research and development and Consultants undertook to provide the necessary funds. The appellant taxpayer, R I S - Christie Ltd., agreed to invest in the project after being approached by Consultants (the Federal Court of Appeal describes it as having invested $230,000 through the numbered company), and it was not disputed that O Inc. received $230,000 under the arrangement in the 1983 taxation year, while Slonimsky and Dorcich agreed to undertake the necessary research. Relying on this contractual expenditure, R I S - Christie Ltd. filed its corporate income tax return for its 1982 taxation year claiming three distinct statutory incentives under the Act: a current deduction for scientific research expenditures in the amount of $160,000 pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Act, a supplementary research allowance of $80,000 pursuant to subsection 37.1(1) and paragraph 37.1(5)(e) of the Act, and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) of $40,000 pursuant to subsection 127(9) of the Act.

The physical execution of the project proceeded in distinct chronological stages across multiple fiscal periods. Phase I of the experimental development began after the first instalment of funds was received in March 1983 and, by the end of 1983, produced a working prototype of the spatial membrane panel intended for field testing in 1984. Following completion of the Phase I prototype, the researchers secured additional financing for Phases II and III in April 1984 and continued development throughout 1984 and 1985. The multi-year investigation ultimately culminated in the filing of an application for a Canadian patent on January 31, 1986, which was formally granted and issued to 589576 Ontario Inc., a successor corporation to O Inc., on April 30, 1991.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Procedural History

The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") audited the claim and issued Notices of Reassessment disallowing the paragraph 37(1)(a) deduction, the subsection 37.1(1) research allowance, and the subsection 127(9) ITC for the 1982 taxation year. As a consequence of the adjustments to the appellant's 1982 taxable income, the Minister also reassessed the appellant's 1983 taxation year by reducing the small business deduction claimed in that year under section 125 of the Act; the Federal Court of Appeal later noted that it was apparently common ground that the research expenditures properly related to the 1983 taxation year rather than 1982 as originally claimed. The Crown's central contention was that the development work conducted on the spatial membrane panel did not constitute "scientific research" (now termed "scientific research and experimental development") within the statutory meaning of section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations.

At trial before the Tax Court of Canada, the Crown tendered an expert witness, Dr. Razaqpur, who articulated a general methodology of scientific research encompassing five sequential stages: formulating the problem, constructing the model, testing the model, deriving a solution from the model, and testing and implementing the solution. The Crown argued that inherent in any systematic scientific investigation is the requirement of "repeatability"—namely, that the researcher must maintain detailed contemporaneous records of experimental conditions, quantitative parameters, and test observations sufficient to enable an independent third party to replicate the exact experiments and verify or falsify the hypothesis. Because R I S - Christie Ltd. and the researchers could not produce comprehensive written test logs documenting each iterative experiment from 1983, the Minister asserted that the project failed to qualify as scientific research.

The Tax Court Judge (Sarchuk T.C.J.) relied principally on the evidence of Daniel Dorcich—tendered by affidavit and cross-examination on that affidavit because his health did not permit him to attend court, rather than as viva voce testimony in court—and found that it confirmed that investigation and experimentation to develop the spatial membrane panel had been conducted during the taxation years in issue and that a new product had been created, and he held that there was some evidence that an engineering uncertainty existed, that a hypothesis was formulated, and that, by testing models, O Inc. resolved the problem and created a practical product embodying a technological advance. Nevertheless, relying on his prior jurisprudence in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (T.C.C.), the Tax Court Judge held that "repeatability"—experiments in which the steps, the changes made, and the results are carefully noted—was an essential attribute of scientific research under Regulation 2900, and that even a less rigorous standard than that applied in pure or applied research would not assist the appellant. Giving no weight to the conclusions of the appellant's expert, Edward Littlejohn, and finding that concluding repeatability had been established would require speculation rather than inference from proven facts, the Tax Court dismissed the appeal for the 1983 taxation year and allowed the 1982 appeal only on an unrelated reserve issue settled by the parties' Partial Consent to Judgment, granting no scientific research relief.
Governing Statutory Framework

During the taxation years under appeal, the substantive and incentive framework for Canadian R&D tax reliefs operated through the integrated operation of the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations. Under paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Act, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada was permitted to deduct expenditures of a current nature made in Canada on scientific research related to the business and directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Originating from 1944 wartime amendments to the Income War Tax Act, section 37 functions as a deliberate statutory exception to the general prohibition against deducting capital outlays under section 18 of the Act, serving the fiscal policy goal of encouraging private sector innovation in Canada. During the transitional years at issue, subsection 37.1(1) and paragraph 37.1(5)(e) of the Act complemented this base deduction by providing an additional research allowance (a super-allowance) equal to 50% of qualified scientific research expenditures exceeding a statutory base period threshold. Concurrently, subsection 127(9) of the Act entitled the taxpayer to claim an Investment Tax Credit calculated as a statutory percentage of qualified expenditures incurred in respect of scientific research and experimental development, directly reducing Part I tax otherwise payable or generating a cash refund for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations.

The substantive technical threshold for these incentives was governed by sections 2900, 2901, and 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations. Subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations—the substance of which was subsequently carried into the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act—defined qualifying work for the purposes of paragraphs 37(7)(b) and 37.1(5)(e) as a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The regulation bifurcated eligible work into three foundational categories: basic research under paragraph 2900(1)(a), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research under paragraph 2900(1)(b), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and development under paragraph 2900(1)(c) (the term used in the Regulation as quoted in both the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal decisions), defined as the use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes. In the current definition in subsection 248(1) of the Act, paragraph (d) explicitly includes directly supporting work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

In interpreting this statutory architecture, the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie expressly declined to undertake a dissertation on the legal meaning of "scientific research" and instead referred readers, for a comprehensive analysis, to the framework set out by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (T.C.C.). That framework established five cumulative criteria—subsequently summarized by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, as the canonical "Five Questions"—requiring the presence of technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures, the formulation of hypotheses aimed at reducing that uncertainty, a systematic methodology following the scientific method, the achievement of a technological advancement, and the maintenance of records of hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progresses.
The Federal Court of Appeal's Final Holding

The Federal Court of Appeal unanimously allowed R I S - Christie Ltd.'s appeal with costs both in the Court of Appeal and in the Tax Court of Canada, set aside the lower court's judgment, and allowed the appeal from the Minister's assessments, having noted that it was apparently common ground that the research expenditures underlying the paragraph 37(1)(a) deduction, the subsection 37.1(1) research allowance, and the subsection 127(9) ITC properly related to the 1983 taxation year.

In delivering the judgment of the Court, Justice Robertson established three binding legal principles in Canadian tax jurisprudence. First, the Court held that what constitutes "scientific research" under the Act and Regulation 2900 is a question of law, or a question of mixed law and fact, reserved exclusively for the Court to decide; expert witnesses play an assistive role in helping the trier of fact comprehend technical evidence, but cannot define the statutory threshold or impose rigid academic documentation rules not enacted by Parliament. Second, the Court rejected absolute documentary "repeatability," holding that while contemporaneous written records are the most reliable evidence of systematic research, the Tax Court erred in law by elevating the repeatability criterion into an inflexible evidentiary bar that automatically disqualifies a taxpayer who lacks complete written test logs. Third, Justice Robertson established the doctrine of the "rebuttable inference": once a court concludes on the evidence that testing was performed, a new product was created, and a genuine technological advancement was achieved, a rebuttable inference is raised that the testing was carried out systematically in compliance with the SR&ED criteria of Regulation 2900.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

Although R I S - Christie Ltd. ultimately prevailed before the Federal Court of Appeal, the protracted sixteen-year dispute—spanning from the initial 1982 investment to the 1998 appellate judgment—was precipitated by severe operational, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies on the part of the taxpayer, compounded by fundamental doctrinal errors committed by the tax authority and the trial court. A rigorous technical examination of the ruling reveals a dual layer of failures: first, the practical compliance failures by the claimant that triggered audit disallowance and defeat at the Tax Court; and second, the legal misinterpretations by the Minister and the trial judge regarding how substantiation interacts with substantive SR&ED eligibility.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and the "Repeatability" Deficit

The primary vulnerability that caused the Minister to disallow the claim and the Tax Court Judge to dismiss the initial appeal was the taxpayer's failure to maintain and produce contemporaneous experimental records from the 1983 Phase I testing. Under the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, and consistent with the FCA's observation in RIS-Christie that documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between tests is the only sure-fire way of establishing systematic research, a claimant is expected to maintain detailed records of hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progresses so that the experimental pathway is verifiable and repeatable.

In RIS-Christie, while engineer Leonid Slonimsky and businessman Daniel Dorcich, with assistants, carried out design calculations, repeated redesigns, and informal shop tests on the spatial membrane panel in 1983 (Dorcich described early experiments as pieces of metal assembled and loaded "to get the feel of the matter," with failed parts thrown into the garbage), the appellant produced only some 39 to 42 pages of sketches and handwritten notes, a synopsis written in 1987, and status reports; the appellant's expert testified that hundreds of further pages of Slonimsky's sketches, calculations, and notes were stored in a barn in Georgetown, but they were never produced, and no structured test logs, test set-ups, specimen data, or analyses correlating results to hypotheses were placed in evidence. When challenged by the Crown's expert witness, Dr. Razaqpur, the appellant could not produce documentary artifacts proving how each specific model was constructed, what numerical loads or thermal variables were applied during individual test runs, or how specific test failures informed subsequent design modifications. This evidentiary vacuum allowed the Minister to argue that, even if a concrete forming panel was eventually fabricated, there was no objective verification that the path taken in 1983 was a "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis" under subsection 2900(1) rather than ad hoc workshop tinkering or routine trial-and-error.
Contractual and Governance Disconnect in Subcontracted and Invested R&D

A critical structural failure underlying the evidentiary gap in RIS-Christie stemmed from the separation between the financing taxpayer claiming the tax credits (R I S - Christie Ltd.) and the technical personnel executing the research (Slonimsky and Dorcich operating through the numbered corporation, O Inc.). Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 248(1) of the Act, expenditures are eligible when scientific research is undertaken directly by or "on behalf of" the taxpayer. However, when R&D is performed by a third-party contractor or an investee research corporation pursuant to a commercial R&D agreement (such as the December 1, 1982 agreement), the statutory onus of proof in tax audits and litigation remains squarely on the claiming taxpayer.

The December 1, 1982 agreement was concluded between Consultants and O Inc., under which O Inc. agreed to perform the research and development of the concrete forming medium and Consultants undertook to provide the necessary funds (O Inc. received $230,000 in 1983); R I S - Christie Ltd. was not itself a party to that agreement, and the Tax Court observed that the agreement contained no information regarding the nature of the research being carried on—nothing in the decision indicates that it required the performers to compile, archive, or deliver contemporaneous SR&ED documentation. Consequently, at trial the corporate appellant was forced to rely principally on Dorcich's affidavit evidence and cross-examination, the expert evidence of Edward Littlejohn (to which the Tax Court gave no weight), some 39 to 42 pages of Slonimsky's sketches and notes, the November 1982 proposal, a synopsis prepared in September 1987, and the patent applied for in 1986 to reconstruct the 1983 experimental methodology.
Fiscal Period Cut-Off and Expenditure Timing Mismatch

The dispute was initially triggered by an accounting and tax timing error by the appellant. Following the agreement executed as of December 1, 1982 between Consultants and O Inc., R I S - Christie Ltd. claimed the $160,000 deduction under paragraph 37(1)(a), the $80,000 research allowance under subsection 37.1(1), and the $40,000 ITC under subsection 127(9) in its 1982 taxation year. However, Phase I of the actual scientific research and experimental development did not commence in earnest until 1983.

Under Canadian tax law governing section 37 and subsection 127(9), prepaid R&D capital contributions or unexpended advances to a research performer cannot be claimed prior to the taxation year in which the qualifying SR&ED work is actually undertaken and the expenditures are incurred for SR&ED purposes. The Minister disallowed the 1982 claims and, as a consequence, reduced the appellant's 1983 small business deduction; before the Tax Court, the second issue was whether any qualifying expenditure was deductible in 1982 or 1983, but the Tax Court never reached it because it found that scientific research had not been established, while the Federal Court of Appeal noted that it was apparently common ground that the expenditures properly related to 1983.
The Tax Court's Legal Error: Conflating Evidentiary Weight with Statutory Eligibility

While the taxpayer's documentation and governance failures created the controversy, the Federal Court of Appeal identified a profound legal error by the Minister and the Tax Court Judge in how they adjudicated those deficiencies. Relying on Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (T.C.C.), the trial judge treated the "repeatability" criterion—defined as the presence of written documentation enabling third parties to repeat the exact experiments—as an essential attribute of scientific research under Regulation 2900; although the trial judge acknowledged that a less rigorous standard might be appropriate for the development of new technology, he held that the evidence would still fall short, and the Federal Court of Appeal characterized this as imposing on the taxpayer an evidentiary burden of documentary proof of test results.

Justice Robertson dismantled this rigid formalism by distinguishing between what must be proved (the statutory elements of Regulation 2900) and how it may be proved under the law of evidence. Subsection 2900(1) requires a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The regulation contains no statutory mandate that experimental evidence must be exclusively documentary. Although the Tax Court Judge framed the point as "some evidence" (and treated the patent as some, but not dispositive, evidence of a new product), the Federal Court of Appeal read his reasons in context as findings—based principally on Dorcich's evidence—that testing had taken place, a new product had been created, and a technological advance had been achieved, and held that, once those findings were made, it was an error to deny the claim solely because documentary evidence satisfying the repeatability criterion was absent.
Second- and Third-Order Implications: The Fragility of the "Rebuttable Inference" in Modern CRA Practice

From a strategic advisory standpoint, senior tax practitioners must recognize the exact doctrinal limits of RIS-Christie when defending modern SR&ED claims before the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Tax Court of Canada. In its current Claim Review Manual (CRM) for Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs), the CRA explicitly incorporates RIS-Christie alongside Northwest Hydraulic and Sass Manufacturing. An analysis of this jurisprudential triad reveals why relying on the RIS-Christie "rebuttable inference" without contemporaneous documentation is a precarious posture for modern taxpayers.

First, the RIS-Christie rebuttable inference that testing was conducted systematically is strictly conditional: it arises once the court is satisfied that testing was undertaken and that a technological advancement was achieved (the FCA separately recognized that a court may also infer systematic research, on the totality of the evidence, where the taxpayer offers a plausible explanation for missing documents, such as research notes accidentally destroyed). In RIS-Christie, the FCA accepted that a technological advance had been achieved in the construction industry—although the Crown's expert disputed that any new technology was developed and the Tax Court treated the patent as some, but not dispositive, evidence—in the form of a novel spatial membrane panel prototype created in 1983 that culminated in a Canadian patent issued in 1991. Conversely, in Sass Manufacturing, the project was abandoned and yielded no technological advancement; without an advancement, no inference arose, and the lack of repeatable test records was fatal to the claim. Similarly, in subsequent Tax Court of Canada decisions such as Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, where projects either failed to resolve a technological uncertainty beyond routine engineering or failed to prove a clear technological advancement over the existing industry benchmark, the absence of rigorous evidence establishing a scientific advancement resulted in complete disallowance.

Second, relying on RIS-Christie exposes failed or incremental R&D projects to severe audit risk. A cornerstone of the Canadian SR&ED program, recognized by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie itself, is that commercial or practical success is not required; failed experiments that advance the company's technological knowledge base by systematically eliminating hypotheses are fully eligible. However, if an experimental program fails to produce a working prototype or patentable device, the taxpayer cannot point to a finished physical artifact to trigger the RIS-Christie inference. For abandoned, failed, or incremental R&D, contemporaneous documentation showing hypothesis formulation, systematic testing, and logical analysis is the primary evidentiary mechanism to distinguish eligible SR&ED from ineligible routine debugging or trial-and-error.

Third, while RIS-Christie prevents the Crown from treating missing test logs as an automatic legal bar at trial when oral testimony and physical breakthroughs are compelling—as recently reaffirmed by the Tax Court in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, where credible oral testimony from the claimant's CEO substantiated frozen pie recipe experimentation—administrative compliance with the CRA remains heavily documentation-driven. Under Chapter 5.12 of the Claim Review Manual, CRA RTAs are instructed to scrutinize claims for inadequate supporting evidence against the record-keeping requirement in subsection 230(1) of the Act, issue formal "Better Books and Records" letters, and, where requested evidence is not provided, disallow the work as unsubstantiated.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen against the taxpayer's specific operational or evidentiary deficiency, the Tax Court's erroneous intermediate ruling, and the authoritative standard of proof established by the Federal Court of Appeal.

headers: Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) Authoritative Standard of Proof

cells: 1. Definition of Scientific Research / SR&ED (Question of Law vs. Fact)
Income Tax Act, s. 37(1)(a), s. 248(1); Income Tax Regulations, s. 2900(1); RIS-Christie.
Allowed the Crown's expert witness (Dr. Razaqpur) to frame the technical critique around textbook academic research stages that the taxpayer's informal records did not mirror.

Accepted the Crown expert's evidence (giving no weight to the appellant's expert, Littlejohn) and adopted the Minister's position that repeatability is an essential attribute of "scientific research" under Regulation 2900, citing its own earlier decision in Sass Manufacturing.

What constitutes SR&ED under the Act is a question of law or mixed law and fact for the Court alone to decide; expert witnesses may only assist the court in understanding technical evidence, not interpret the statute.
2. Technological Risk or Uncertainty
Income Tax Regulations, s. 2900(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 1); CW Agencies.

Although Dorcich testified that Phase I began with a review and analysis of technical literature and Canadian and U.S. patent applications on existing concrete forming systems, no formal written baseline was produced, and an independent architectural engineering review of the November 1982 proposal (dated January 18, 1983) concluded that a much more comprehensive feasibility study appeared to be required.
Found that Dorcich outlined the engineering uncertainty quite adequately and that there was some evidence an engineering uncertainty existed, but held that the claim failed on repeatability.

Technological uncertainty exists where a problem cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; it may be established through credible testimony and context showing the limits of existing technology.
3. Formulation of Hypotheses Aimed at Reducing Uncertainty
Income Tax Regulations, s. 2900(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2); RIS-Christie.

Did not produce written design iterations or problem-formulation records detailing the hypotheses tested during Phase I in 1983 (Dorcich believed sketches of alternatives were probably made but discarded, and said the reasons for redesigns were noted on drawings that were never produced).

Accepted that there was some evidence a hypothesis was formulated, but held that the absence of recorded test set-ups, methodology, data, and correlation of data to the original hypothesis meant repeatability was not established.

Hypotheses must be formulated to reduce or eliminate the technological uncertainty, but their formulation and iterative refinement can be proven through credible oral testimony and progressive prototype evolution.
4. Systematic Investigation or Search by Experiment or Analysis
Income Tax Regulations, s. 2900(1)(a)–(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3); RIS-Christie.
Failed to retain comprehensive written experimental logs or quantitative test data from 1983 showing step-by-step model testing and analysis.

Held that, although investigation and experimentation were conducted and a new product was created, inferring the essential element of repeatability from the evidence would require speculation, so the work was not shown to be scientific research.

Once evidence proves that testing was performed, a new product was created, and a technological advancement resulted, a rebuttable inference arises that the testing was conducted systematically in compliance with Regulation 2900.
5. Technological Advancement (Creation of New or Improved Product/Process)
Income Tax Regulations, s. 2900(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4); Sass Manufacturing distinguished.

Relied on end-stage outcomes (the 1983 working prototype, 1986 patent filing, and 1991 patent grant) rather than intermediate technical progression records (the June 30 and December 16, 1983 status reports in evidence provided no real assistance on the nature of the research).

Found some evidence that a practical product embodying a technological advance was created (treating the patent as some, but not dispositive, evidence of a new product), yet failed to give legal effect to this finding by subordinating it to the repeatability criterion from Sass Manufacturing.

Achieving a proven technological advancement (unlike the abandoned, fruitless project in Sass Manufacturing) is powerful substantive proof of SR&ED that triggers the rebuttable inference of systematic research.
6. Repeatability and Contemporaneous Record-Keeping
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); RIS-Christie; Income Tax Act, s. 230(1).
Could not adduce recorded test parameters enabling an independent third party to repeat the exact 1983 experiments and reproduce the results.

Treated "repeatability" as an essential attribute of scientific research and, while acknowledging that a less rigorous standard might apply to the development of new technology, held that the lack of recorded test information was fatal on the evidence before it.

Documentary evidence of repeatability is the clearest proof of SR&ED, but is not an absolute legal prerequisite; credible oral testimony and physical/patent evidence can satisfy the burden where the absence of documents is plausibly explained or where the research is established to have led to a technological advancement.
7. Timing of Expenditures & Third-Party R&D Governance
Income Tax Act, s. 37(1)(a), s. 37.1(1), s. 127(9); Income Tax Regulations, s. 2900.

Claimed the $160k deduction, $80k allowance, and $40k ITC in 1982 following the Dec 1, 1982 funding agreement between Consultants and O Inc. (to which the appellant was not a party), whereas O Inc. received the funds and Phase I research occurred in 1983; nothing in the decision indicates any contractual requirement for O Inc. to deliver R&D logs.

Dismissed the 1983 appeal on the repeatability ruling without reaching the timing issue; the 1982 appeal was allowed only on an unrelated reserve issue under the parties' Partial Consent to Judgment, with no SR&ED relief.

Allowed the appeal from the Minister's assessments with costs, noting that it was apparently common ground that the expenditures related to the 1983 taxation year (when the Phase I SR&ED was actually performed); the judgment does not itself specify the amounts of the s. 37(1)(a) deduction, s. 37.1(1) allowance, and s. 127(9) ITC to be allowed.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate jurisprudence of RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen—and its interplay with Northwest Hydraulic, Sass Manufacturing, and the CRA's Claim Review Manual—into actionable tax and engineering governance, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers can proactively remediate the exact contractual, timing, and documentation pitfalls identified in the ruling.
Case Study 1: Subcontracted Civil Engineering and Composite Structural Forming (Overcoming the Investor/Performer Disconnect, Period Cut-Off, and Repeatability Deficit)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Apex Precast Structures Ltd. ("Apex"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Mississauga, Ontario, specializes in modular bridge and tunnel infrastructure. Seeking to develop an ultra-lightweight, self-insulating Basalt-Fibre Geopolymer Concrete (BFGC) stay-in-place structural form panel that eliminates steel rebar corrosion while achieving a compressive strength exceeding 60 MPa in sub-zero curing conditions, Apex enters into a Research and Development Agreement on December 10, 2025, with GeoMatrix Engineering Inc. ("GeoMatrix"), an arm's-length Canadian structural engineering boutique led by two professional engineers.

Under the agreement, Apex transfers an upfront lump sum of $450,000 to GeoMatrix on December 15, 2025, for Phase I prototype development. Apex's fiscal year-end is December 31. GeoMatrix orders raw materials in late December 2025 but conducts all chemical formulation, thermal-curing simulations, and hydraulic load-testing between January 15, 2026, and September 30, 2026. GeoMatrix's engineers test 18 different alkali-activator ratios and basalt-mesh geometries on their shop floor, discarding failed panels into a scrap bin without recording intermediate load-deflection curves or curing temperatures, before arriving at a successful prototype in September 2026 and filing a provisional Canadian patent application in November 2026. Apex attempts to claim the full $450,000 as a qualified SR&ED expenditure under subsection 37(1) and claim a 35% refundable ITC under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) on its T2 corporate income tax return and Form T661 for the taxation year ended December 31, 2025.

This operational structure triggers three acute pitfalls identified in RIS-Christie. First, Apex commits a fiscal cut-off violation: mirroring R I S - Christie Ltd.'s disallowed 1982 claim for 1983 research, Apex is claiming a prepaid December 2025 outlay for SR&ED work not performed until the 2026 taxation year. Second, Apex suffers from a performer documentation custody gap: like the December 1, 1982 agreement between Consultants and O Inc. under which the R I S - Christie Ltd. project was funded, Apex's contract with GeoMatrix contains no legal covenant requiring GeoMatrix to maintain or turn over contemporaneous experimental logs, leaving Apex vulnerable when a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) issues a Request for Information (RFI) or exercises third-party audit powers under subsection 231.1(1) of the Act and Chapter 5.4 of the Claim Review Manual. Third, GeoMatrix's erasure of intermediate failures destroys documentary repeatability: by scrapping the 17 failed panels without recording test parameters, GeoMatrix leaves Apex unable to demonstrate step-by-step systematic progression. If the CRA RTA disputes that the September 2026 panel is a genuine technological advancement—arguing instead that combining basalt mesh with geopolymer binders is routine engineering—Apex will lose the RIS-Christie rebuttable inference and face total disallowance under Sass Manufacturing and Joel Theatrical Rigging.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Fiscal Timing Alignment

Apex and its tax counsel must immediately align expenditure recognition with physical SR&ED performance under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the Act. Rather than claiming the $450,000 lump sum in the 2025 taxation year based solely on the December 10, 2025 contract execution date, Apex must segregate expenditures by the exact fiscal period in which the underlying SR&ED work is performed in Canada. Any portion of the $450,000 representing unconsumed prepaid advances at December 31, 2025, must be deferred and claimed on Form T661 in the 2026 taxation year when GeoMatrix actually executes the Phase I systematic investigation. Furthermore, Apex must establish a joint SR&ED Technical Steering Committee comprising Apex's Vice-President of Engineering and GeoMatrix's lead engineers, meeting bi-weekly to review and formally approve experimental test protocols before new physical pours are authorized.
Step 2: Overhauling Contract Terms via an SR&ED Performer Schedule

To prevent the third-party evidentiary disconnect suffered in RIS-Christie, Apex must amend the December 10, 2025 R&D Agreement with GeoMatrix to incorporate a mandatory SR&ED Compliance and Documentation Schedule containing five enforceable legal covenants. First, the Statement of Work (SOW) must be tied directly to subsection 248(1) of the Act, defining the contracted services not merely as delivering a working BFGC panel prototype—which risks characterizing the contract as the acquisition of a commercial product rather than the performance of SR&ED—but as performing a systematic investigation by means of experiment and analysis to resolve specified technological uncertainties regarding micro-crack propagation in alkali-activated basalt matrices below −20°C. Second, the contract must expressly stipulate that all research is undertaken "on behalf of" Apex within the meaning of paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Act and paragraph (d) of the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act, that Apex bears the financial and technical risk of experimental failure, and that GeoMatrix waives any independent right to claim SR&ED tax credits on the funded work.

Third, to enforce documentation discipline, the $450,000 consideration must be structured into four progressive tranche payments, with a mandatory 20% contractual holdback on each tranche that is released only upon GeoMatrix uploading complete, timestamped experimental test logs, raw sensor data, and failure analyses into Apex's digital repository. Fourth, the agreement must require GeoMatrix to provide itemized invoicing separating eligible Canadian labour, materials consumed or transformed in testing, and ineligible overhead, enabling Apex to accurately compute the statutory 80% arm's-length subcontractor expenditure inclusion for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9). Fifth, the contract must include a binding audit cooperation and witness covenant obligating GeoMatrix's key engineers to attend CRA RTA on-site interviews under Chapter 5.6.4 of the Claim Review Manual and provide viva voce testimony before the Tax Court of Canada for a period of seven years post-completion.
Step 3: Technical Documentation Architecture Establishing Benchmark and Uncertainty

To satisfy Questions 1 and 2 of the Northwest Hydraulic test referred to in RIS-Christie, Apex must require GeoMatrix to author a Phase 0 Baseline Technological Assessment Report prior to mixing the first batch of concrete in January 2026. This document must cite peer-reviewed civil engineering literature, Canadian Highway Bridge Design Code (CSA S6) standards, and commercial vendor specifications to prove that existing Portland cement and standard fly-ash geopolymers suffer severe brittle delamination and thermal bridging when cast in thin-walled spatial membranes below −20°C. By documenting the exact limits of the current state-of-the-art knowledge base through literature reviews and feasibility analyses, Apex establishes the industry benchmark and preemptively defeats any CRA contention that the work was resolvable through routine engineering or standard procedures.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Repeatability Protocol

To satisfy both Dr. Razaqpur's five-stage scientific model cited in RIS-Christie (formulating the problem, constructing the model, testing the model, deriving a solution, and testing and implementing the solution) and the Tax Court's repeatability standard, Apex must institute a standardized Experimental Run Matrix (ERM) for all 18 prototype batches. Under this protocol, every batch from Run #01 through Run #18 is assigned a unique identifier linked to an explicit Hypothesis Statement, such as testing whether increasing the sodium silicate-to-sodium hydroxide molar ratio from 2.0 to 2.5 while tensioning a bi-axial 25 mm basalt grid at 15 kN will prevent thermal micro-fissuring during 72-hour hydration without exceeding a panel thickness of 40 mm.

For each run, engineers must log exact environmental and material parameters—including ambient humidity, curing chamber temperature profile, molarity, aggregate particle-size distribution, and hydraulic actuator load rates—so that any independent structural engineer could repeat the exact experiment and verify the findings. Crucially, before the 17 failed panels are scrapped, engineers must capture high-resolution digital photographs of fracture planes, export telemetry files from the universal testing machine showing load-deflection failure points, and record an Analytical Conclusion explaining why the hypothesis failed and how that newly generated scientific knowledge dictates the variable adjustment in the subsequent run. When combined with the November 2026 patent filing, this documentation renders Apex's claim unassailable: it secures both the RIS-Christie rebuttable inference arising from the patented technological advancement and complete documentary proof of systematic repeatability.
Case Study 2: Industrial Automation and Adaptive Vision Control (Defending Iterative Shop-Floor Development Where Commercial Abandonment Precludes the RIS-Christie Inference)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

KinemaTech Industrial Controls Inc. ("KinemaTech"), a manufacturing automation firm located in Montreal, Quebec, undertakes an internal R&D project during its 2025 taxation year to develop a real-time, edge-computed 3D laser-profilometry and machine-learning feedback controller capable of dynamically reconfiguring a robotic stamping line to produce 180 distinct architectural panel geometries from 600 modular sub-components within a three-hour changeover window, with zero calibration scrap.

KinemaTech's team of four software and mechatronics engineers spends 4,200 hours writing custom C++ edge-inference algorithms and testing optical sensor arrays directly on a live commercial production line between production shifts. Because the engineers operate in an Agile development environment focused on rapid shop-floor deployment, they overwrite failed code branches in their repository without commit notes, do not maintain formal test plans, and log all their time to a single generic accounting code ("Project 2025-Vision"). After ten months and $680,000 in salary and sensor prototype expenditures, the team discovers that harmonic vibrations from the heavy stamping presses cause irreducible phase-noise in the laser profilometers above 120 strokes per minute. Unable to achieve the target sub-millimetre tolerance at commercial speeds, KinemaTech abandons the laser-profilometry architecture at the end of 2025 without a working commercial product or patent. Upon audit of KinemaTech's 2025 Form T661 claim, the CRA RTA proposes a 100% disallowance, citing Sass Manufacturing and arguing that because the project was abandoned with no technological advancement and lacks repeatable test logs, the work was merely unsubstantiated shop-floor debugging.

KinemaTech's posture exposes the company to three severe legal vulnerabilities under RIS-Christie. First, KinemaTech loses the RIS-Christie rebuttable inference due to project abandonment: in RIS-Christie, Justice Robertson explicitly distinguished Sass Manufacturing on the basis that the Sass project was abandoned and produced no technological advance, whereas RIS-Christie yielded a working prototype and patent. Because KinemaTech abandoned its laser-profilometry system without a viable commercial device, a trial judge will not automatically infer that the testing was systematic from a finished product alone. Second, by overwriting failed algorithm iterations and failing to record sensor calibration trials, KinemaTech cannot demonstrate to a third party how its testing progressed systematically from hypothesis to analysis, failing both the repeatability standard and Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic. Third, testing on a live production line and logging all hours to a single cost code leaves KinemaTech unable to separate eligible experimental development and directly supporting work under paragraph (d) of the definition in subsection 248(1) of the Act from commercial production and quality control or routine testing, which paragraphs (i) and (f) of that definition exclude.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance to Separate SR&ED from Shop-Floor Production

To prevent the CRA from classifying the 4,200 engineering hours as routine production maintenance or commercial trial-and-error, KinemaTech must establish a formal SR&ED Project Charter and Stage-Gate Governance Protocol at project inception. The governance charter must explicitly draw a boundary between standard engineering integration—such as configuring off-the-shelf programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and mounting commercial cameras, which is excluded routine engineering—and the core SR&ED project aimed at resolving the systemic technological uncertainty of coupled optical-mechanical signal distortion under high-frequency impulse loading. Shop-floor experimental windows must be formally scheduled as dedicated Experimental Trial Blocks, signed off by the Plant Manager and Lead R&D Engineer, during which the stamping line is removed from commercial inventory production and operated strictly as an experimental test rig.
Step 2: Proving Technological Advancement in an Abandoned Project to Neutralize Sass Manufacturing

The critical legal lesson from the FCA's comparison of RIS-Christie and Sass Manufacturing is that an abandoned commercial project can still qualify for SR&ED tax credits in Canada, provided the taxpayer proves that the systematic investigation generated new scientific or technological knowledge—that is, a technological advancement in understanding the underlying physical or algorithmic phenomena, even if the target commercial product proved unfeasible.

KinemaTech must restructure its technical narrative and documentation to demonstrate that discovering and mathematically characterizing the exact harmonic resonance threshold (press-frame harmonics above 38 Hz creating 0.4 mm structural aliasing that corrupts coherent laser interferometry) constituted a genuine technological advancement. By authoring a formal Technical Advancement Post-Mortem Report that documents the analytical proof of why edge-computed laser profilometry fails in high-impulse stamping environments—knowledge that was not available in the public domain or sensor manufacturer datasheets—KinemaTech establishes a valid technological advancement under subsection 248(1) and restores the substantive foundation required by RIS-Christie.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Version-Control Architecture Preserving Repeatability

To eliminate the repeatability failure that doomed the taxpayer at the Tax Court level in RIS-Christie, KinemaTech must configure its software and hardware engineering workflows to automatically generate contemporaneous, repeatable experimental records without imposing bureaucratic friction on its engineers. First, KinemaTech must enforce immutable Git branching and tagging for all experimental hypotheses, prohibiting engineers from overwriting failed code branches. Every experimental algorithm iteration must be committed to a dedicated branch tagged with an SR&ED Experiment ID (such as SRED-2025-EXP-14-Kalman-Filter-Dealiasing), and each pull request or branch closure must require a mandatory template capturing four fields matching Dr. Razaqpur's scientific model in RIS-Christie: the Technological Uncertainty Addressed, the Mathematical or Algorithmic Hypothesis, the Empirical Test Configuration and Sensor Dataset Link, and the Analytical Results and Conclusion.

Second, KinemaTech must implement automated telemetry and sensor dataset archiving by retaining raw oscilloscope traces, accelerometer vibration logs, and 3D point-cloud error matrices from each shop-floor Experimental Trial Block in an immutable data repository indexed by Experiment ID. This architecture ensures that an independent expert witness or CRA RTA can replay the exact sensor dataset through the archived Git code branch and replicate the exact experimental results, satisfying the strictest interpretation of the repeatability criterion.
Step 4: Granular Time-Tracking and Support-Activity Allocation Under Subsection 248(1)

To substantiate the $680,000 expenditure claim under section 37 and subsection 127(9) and address the CRA's scrutiny of the nature and extent of work conducted in the tax period, KinemaTech must replace its single generic project code with a granular activity-tracking protocol aligned with paragraph (d) of the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act. Engineers must log time contemporaneously across distinct activity classifications that link directly to the experimental lifecycle: logging mathematical modelling and hypothesis formulation to 2025-SR-01; logging experimental C++ dealiasing coding and test-rig sensor mount fabrication that is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core experimentation to 2025-SR-02; logging controlled shop-floor experimental trial execution and data collection to 2025-SR-03; and logging point-cloud divergence analysis and the drafting of the Technical Advancement Post-Mortem Report to 2025-SR-04. Concurrently, all routine PLC wiring, operator training, and standard commercial production runs must be segregated into an excluded cost code (2025-NON-SRED) and stripped from the Form T661 claim.
